To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mutated proteins arising from sommatic mutations in tumors are a promising target for cancer immunotherapy and that vaccination with mutated peptides induces polyvalent, mutation-specific effector and regulatory T cell responses.
vaccination with mutated driver gene peptides induces polyvalent, mutation-specific effector and regulatory T cell responses that can be exploited for tumor therapy.

vaccination with mutated peptides derived from driver gene mutations in colorectal cancer can be a promising approach to induce tumor-specific effector T cell responses, but the success of this strategy can be hampered due to the concomitant induction of tumor-specific Tregs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel, personalized immunotherapeutic strategy that is based on the vaccination with a panel of mutated peptides.
the development of cancer mutation-specific immunotherapy.
the development of a new therapeutic approach to combat gastrointestinal tumors, namely the vaccination against driver gene mutations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mutated peptides can be used as tumor-specific targets, but the immunogenicity has to be balanced to prevent tumor-promoting Treg responses.
vaccination with mutated peptides induces polyfunctional effector T cells that can target tumor cells.
the vaccination with mutated long peptides is a promising immunotherapeutic strategy, however, it has to be carefully balanced to avoid Treg induction and to maximize effector T cell induction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the feasibility of a vaccination approach with mutated proteins in cancer patients.
vaccination with multiple mutated peptides can induce polyvalent effector T cell responses against mutated proteins.

we have identified a panel of immunogenic mutated peptides that are able to induce a polyfunctional T cell response in mice, but also that the immunogenicity of the mutated peptides may be too strong to allow an effective tumor therapy in mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mutated driver genes can be used as targets for immunotherapy.
long peptides comprising driver gene mutations are promising targets for active cancer immunotherapy.
vaccination against mutated proteins can elicit polyvalent, mutation-specific effector CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
